A2.text:
Sevinj is thirty-five. She grew up in Ganja, but now she lives in Baku. Last weekend, she visited Ganja for a friend's wedding. On Sunday morning, she walked to her old yard.

She stopped next to the playground. The old green swing was still there! Sevinj remembered the day she fell from it. She was seven. She remembered it like it was yesterday. She still has a small scar on her knee.

Sevinj sat on a bench. She felt a lot of nostalgia. “Children grow up so fast,” she thought. Her grandmother was very strict. She always said, “Come home before dark!” Her cousin Elnur was spoiled. He had a bicycle, a football and every new toy. And Sevinj had an imaginary friend. His name was Bubu, and he lived under the swing.

A little girl came to the playground. She tried to sit on the swing, but it was too high for her.

“Can you help me?” the girl asked.

“Of course,” Sevinj said. “This is child's play.” She lifted the girl onto the swing and pushed her gently.

“Higher!” the girl laughed.

“Be careful,” Sevinj said. “I fell from this swing once.”

The girl looked at her. “Did you have a friend here too?”

Sevinj smiled. “Yes,” she said. “His name was Bubu.”

B1.text:
Sevinj had not been back to her childhood yard in Ganja for almost twenty years. She grew up in a five-storey building near Javad Khan Street, and when a school friend invited her to a wedding there, she decided to stay an extra day. On Sunday morning, before her train, she walked around the corner and stopped.

The playground was still there. Somebody had painted the fence blue, but the old green swing hung from the same metal frame. Sevinj remembered the afternoon she fell off it like it was yesterday: flying too high, letting go for a second, the gravel, the blood, her grandmother running out in her slippers. The scar on her knee was still there too, a small white line.

She sat on a bench and let herself take a trip down memory lane. Her grandmother had been strict — homework before play, home before dark, no arguments. Her cousin Elnur, on the other hand, was hopelessly spoiled; he got a new bicycle every summer and never shared it. And there was Bubu, the imaginary friend who lived under the swing and agreed with everything she said. She hadn't thought about Bubu for years. Strange, she thought, how nostalgia can arrive so suddenly.

A little girl in a red jacket ran into the playground and tried to climb onto the swing. It was too high for her.

“Can you lift me?” she asked.

“That's child's play,” said Sevinj, and lifted her up. She pushed, gently at first.

“Higher!”

“Hold on with both hands,” Sevinj said. “I fell off this swing when I was your age.”

The girl thought about this seriously. Then she whispered, “Don't tell anyone, but my friend lives under here. He's invisible.”

Sevinj had to look away for a moment. “Say hello to him from me,” she said. “Tell him Bubu says hi.”

B2.text:
It took a wedding to bring Sevinj back to Ganja. She had left at fifteen, when her parents moved to Baku, and in the twenty years since, her childhood had shrunk into a handful of photographs and a story she told at parties. But the morning after the celebration, with three hours before her train, she found her feet carrying her, almost without permission, towards the five-storey building near Javad Khan Street.

The playground had survived. Someone had repainted the fence a cheerful blue and replaced the sandpit with rubber tiles, yet the old green swing still creaked on its rusting frame. She could recall the afternoon she fell from it like it was yesterday: the thrill of flying higher than any of the boys, the reckless decision to let go at the top, the gravel, the blood, her grandmother sprinting across the yard in her house slippers. She touched her knee through her jeans. The scar was still there, a pale crescent.

She sat down on a bench and allowed herself to take a trip down memory lane. Her grandmother had been famously strict — homework before play, indoors before the streetlights, no negotiation. Her cousin Elnur, by contrast, was spoiled beyond repair, a boy who received a new bicycle every summer and regarded sharing as a form of theft. And then there was Bubu, an imaginary friend of enormous patience who lived beneath the swing and approved of all her decisions. She hadn't spared him a thought in decades. Nostalgia, she reflected, was less a feeling than an ambush.

A small girl in a red jacket marched into the playground and attempted to scale the swing, which was clearly built for someone taller.

“Could you lift me?” she demanded.

“Child's play,” said Sevinj, and did.

“Higher!”

“Both hands on the chains,” Sevinj warned. “I fell off this exact swing when I was about your age.”

The child weighed this information gravely. Then she leaned back and confided, in a stage whisper, “My friend lives under here. Grown-ups can't see him.”

Sevinj found that she needed to examine the rooftops for a moment. When she trusted her voice again, she said, “Then please give him a message. Tell him Bubu says it's good to know the place is in safe hands.”
